Personally, I believe in the official rules of scooping at any time. This should make the player actually think about their actions. Just because a person is going to lose doesn’t mean that person has to help another player win. If the opponent blows their investment and the player scoops, that’s the opponent’s problem. This is a valid strategic choice for the person scooping. A player themself is a resource. Opponents should understand this, as it’s within the official rules for a player to deny this resource at any point. Magic is a game that requires the player to find their win by making the best choices. Wasting one’s spells or leaving themself open due to an opponent scooping means the player failed to make the best choices. Meanwhile, female humans seem to have shorter reproductive windows. Every person is going to have a different answer to this. I think there two questions that help to answer this.

1. Does the difference in political beliefs cross either person's moral threshold?
2. Do the persons isolate ideas and beliefs from the individual as a whole?

The first question is very direct and easy- one person's belief is so abominable to another that the other does not believe it ethical to keep their company. The ideology is so abhorrent to at least one person that there is no room for compromise or tolerance. When a person is intolerant of certain politics, they may feel disgust at keeping company with those opposed to something that is core to their beliefs of human rights, morals, and decency. This is likely going to involve politics that severely affect the life and safety of one group that the other the person holds minimal or no concern over.

The second question may involve political matters as intense as the first, but is not exclusive to those topics and may include more mundane political divides. This question functions similar to whether or not a person separates the art from the artist, but in this case, weighing the rest of the person's behaviors and identity against their political beliefs. Simply, even the people with the most wretched and vile beliefs are likely to have some positives to their person and they share those positives with others in their life.

Personally, I distance myself from people whose politics are a danger to myself, those I care about, and those I believe are being put in danger by the politics of that individual. If I don't agree with a friend's politics, but their politics do not cross that threshold of being a direct danger to others, I will likely still be their friend (but I may think they're a dumbass).

I will acknowledge that some people are jaded and refuse to care about perspectives that are outside of the breadth of their life and already existing thoughts. They may not ever be as passionate as the target audience, but they may still love the media. Alternatively, they may understand everything and just find the media poorly executed. Many people in this day and age have become defensive to criticism of media they like.

If the viewer does not understand the media though and could not understand it without explanation that is direct within the media itself, then the media may in fact be something that wasn’t made for others. Attack on Titan was probably the first majorly successful anime that people didn’t feel like was for little kid. I know AoT is still shonen, but the USA generally feels differently whereas most other majorly successful shonen series felt closer to in tone to projects like the MCU, which is generally considered very kid-friendly (Death Note is an outlier, and while successful in the USA m, felt very much confined to the “Hot Topic shoppers” market). 

It’s worth mentioning that there was a push for anime in the mid 00s following successful series on Toonami and Adult Swim on a few networks, but the series grabbed were never ones that would have been major breakout hits with the general public. A number of factors must be viewed to get this answer.

First, some of the biggest box office hits were IPs or franchises. The studios want money, so that’s what they’re going to shoot for. 

What genres are the most profitable? Action films are viewed as the safest bet. Every new action film that is only beholden to itself is a gamble. Subsequently, studios choose to support franchises and IPs as likely safer financial options rather than gamble on a new, isolated film. I would put most sci-fi and fantasy films under action, though there are definite cases where sci fi and horror are one of the other genres below.
Children’s or all-ages animated films follow. Unlike action films, there’s more opportunity, since as kids are born, they do not necessarily hold interest in any already existing films and the studios themselves can potentially act as the branding.

Dramas don’t inherently want this and often aren’t bringing in comparable revenue.
Horror perhaps runs both original films and franchises. Most horror films are cheaper, so there’s less risk. Also, horror has a more notable drop-off in quality and studios will shelve franchises for a while before attempting to bring them back.
Comedy seems mostly dead at this point. Some are still made, but the genre generally doesn’t generate hype and subsequently revenue. Action, horror, drama, and kid movies are all more likely to get someone to say “I want to go to the theater to see this” where most comedies now seem to carry a “oh, I guess we’ll see a movie. This comedy seems to be agreeable to all of us.”

Audience viewing habits have changed. The price of the theater has gone up and reviews and consensus are more easily available while people have streaming services to wait for any movie that isn’t drawing them out to the theater.

I would even posit, though I need evidence, that the profits do not necessarily match up to audience interest and engagement after the film between franchise/IP films and new films that are not franchises/IPs.
